newsitem.title: USA: States pave way for bond sale statements on-line.
newsitem.headline: States pave way for bond sale statements on-line.

text.p: Twenty-seven states now have on-line exemptions that allow municipal issuers to circulate bond offering statements on the internet without running afoul of blue sky laws, a member of one of the nation's largest bond counsel firms said Friday.
Those laws require that securities be registered with state officials before they can be offered for sale in any given state.

When issuers first proposed putting their bond documents on the internet for investor convenience, bond attorneys cautioned against it, fearing the documents would be construed as an illegal sales offer if internet users in other states read them.
The problem was unique to munis, which are often bought only in the state where they are issued.

Under the exemptions, the bond documents are not considered an offer to sell securities unless the bonds are registered in the state where the internet user resides, said Constance LeLouis of Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP told the Bond Buyer Southeast Public Finance Conference.
Less than two years ago, only four states had such exemptions, LeLouis said.
"The movement here is definitely showing a trend that this is going to be a widespread practice in the future," LeLouis said.
In states that still do not have the exemption "You still have to register the security in that state before it could be sold," LeLouis said.

Other members of a muni on-line panel at the conference said they are beginning to use private computer networks to produce and distribute bond documents more efficiently, saving printing and express mail costs for the lengthy documents.

The savings can be considerable, said John Peterson president of Government Finance Group Inc. He gave the example of a complicated three-part issue that took a year to complete and involved 33 underwriters, lawyers and other participants.
During that year, Peterson said, his firm spent $50,000 on express mail to overnight documents and revisions to all the parties.
"We just generate a hell of a lot of paper," he said.

Creating the documents via private on-line networks also allows issuers to link in rating agncies and bond insurers earlier in the process, seeking their advice as the deal is still being structured, other panelists said.
"That will transfer to a lower price for credit enhancement," said Kathleen McDonough, managing director of AMBAC Indemnity Corp.
